overview.text: René Magritte (1898–1967) was a Belgian painter associated with Surrealism, a movement that questioned fixed meanings and ordinary logic. He often painted familiar things in a clear, realistic style, then arranged or labeled them in surprising ways that made viewers question what they were seeing. In The Treachery of Images (1929), a carefully painted pipe appears above the words “This is not a pipe”: the painting shows an image of a pipe, not a usable object. Magritte’s visual puzzles explored how images, words, and objects relate to one another. His distinctive approach made painting a way to challenge assumptions about reality and invite viewers to think as well as look.

key_facts.text: Magritte was born in Belgium in 1898 and died in 1967.
He developed Surrealist paintings using familiar, recognizable subjects while questioning ordinary assumptions and fixed meanings.

The Treachery of Images (1929) depicts a pipe with a caption that says it is not a pipe; LACMA describes it as a key Surrealist work about the difference between an image and the object it represents.
In The Human Condition (1933), an easel holds a landscape painting in front of a window, creating uncertainty about where the view outside ends and the painted image begins.
During his time in Paris, Magritte investigated the relationship between text and image; a MoMA audio guide describes a painting that pairs words with images in unexpected ways.
